The South Georgia icefish (Pseudochaenichthys georgianus) is a channichthyid notothenioid inhabiting the frigid continental shelf waters surrounding South Georgia and the Antarctic Peninsula, notable among vertebrates for lacking hemoglobin in its blood. Newly hatched larvae emerge at a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.045 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.045 grams], a value derived from an egg diameter of about 4.4 millimeters, reflecting the large, yolk-rich eggs typical of Antarctic notothenioids that must sustain slow-developing embryos in near-freezing water. At a water temperature of -0.1 °C [T = -0.1 °C], the age at birth reaches approximately 60 days [ab = approximately 60 days], an extended incubation period consistent with the depressed metabolic rates characteristic of polar ectotherms.

Juvenile icefish grow slowly in the cold, oxygen-rich waters of the Southern Ocean, a pace of development typical of Antarctic notothenioids that rely on elevated blood plasma volume rather than hemoglobin for oxygen transport. Sexual maturation differs modestly between the sexes: females reach the total length at puberty for females of 47.5 centimeters [Lp = 47.5 centimeters], while males mature at a slightly smaller total length at puberty for males of 46.5 centimeters [Lp = 46.5 centimeters]. At these respective sizes, females attain a wet weight at puberty for females of approximately 1,300 grams [Wwp = approximately 1,300 grams], while males attain a somewhat lower wet weight at puberty for males of approximately 1,200 grams [Wwp = approximately 1,200 grams].

Adult body size also differs between the sexes, with females reaching an ultimate total length for females of 59 centimeters [Li = 59 centimeters] and males reaching a slightly smaller ultimate total length for males of 56 centimeters [Li = 56 centimeters]. The ultimate wet weight of this species reaches approximately 2,800 grams [Wwi = approximately 2,800 grams], a substantial body mass supported by the lipid-rich tissues characteristic of icefish, which store energy reserves as fat rather than relying on red blood cells for oxygen delivery.

Reproductive output in the South Georgia icefish is considerable for a polar notothenioid. At the stable thermal regime of -0.1 °C [T = -0.1 °C], the maximum reproductive rate reaches approximately 49 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 49 eggs per day], reflecting a strategy of producing a modest number of large, well-provisioned eggs suited to the slow embryonic development imposed by near-freezing water temperatures. Longevity in this species reaches a maximum of approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years] at the same reference temperature, a considerable lifespan that is consistent with the generally slow pace of life documented among cold-water Antarctic notothenioid fishes at a temperature of -0.1 °C [T = -0.1 °C].
